samples.question: Somewhere in this picture there are exactly two panels drawn with heavy black frames, standing apart from one another, and every pale grey mark outside those two frames is inert decoration that means nothing. The left panel is the rule table. Its top row holds three dot glyphs, one in each of its three right-hand columns; a dot glyph is one, two or three small black dots, and only the number of dots matters, never their arrangement. Underneath that top row the table has four rows. Each row starts, in its leftmost cell, with a coloured disc, and that disc is the row's own colour; the four rows carry four different colours. The other three cells of a row hold coloured discs as well, one under each dot glyph. The table is used as a lookup: if the colour you are holding is the colour that starts a row, and the glyph you are applying has n dots, then the colour you are holding is replaced by the disc that sits in that row in the column whose top-row glyph also has n dots. The right panel is the program. At the top of it, on its own and encircled by a heavy black ring, sits a single coloured disc: that is the colour you start out holding. Below the ring, separated by thin black lines, are four cells stacked one above another, and each of them holds one dot glyph. Those four glyphs are applied one after another, starting with the glyph in the top cell and working downwards, each one replacing the colour you hold by the colour the table looks up for it. The two panels may sit at slightly different places from picture to picture, and the four colours in play are always red, amber, green and blue. After all four glyphs of the program have been applied, which colour are you holding? Answer with one of red, amber, green or blue.
